## Paper

## Abstract

Non-Abelian geometric phases offer fault-tolerant unitary operations that are essential for holonomic quantum computation. While the “all-geometric” approach has successfully enabled robust control of atoms, ions, and electrons in various quantum systems, its photonic implementations have remained limited by a lack of tunability—an essential feature for modern classical or quantum optical information processing. Here, we demonstrate non-volatile multilevel tunable generic special-orthogonal (SO) geometric phases on a multilayer silicon photonic platform incorporating the phase-change material (PCM) of Sb₂Se₃. By toggling Sb₂Se₃ between crystalline and amorphous states, we dynamically control the number of degenerate states involved in the holonomy, enabling switching between different holonomic paths and SO(m) geometric transformations. Our results bridge the key gap between robust geometric-phase control and in-memory reconfigurable photonics, establishing a paradigm for fault-tolerant, high-dimensional operations in integrated optical systems.

---

## Introduction

The non-Abelian geometric phase is well known for its inherent robustness in realizing unitary transformations. Building upon the foundational work on the Berry phase1, Wilczek and Zee pointed out that a matrix-valued geometric phase can emerge from the adiabatic evolution of degenerate quantum states2. Unlike the dynamic phase, which depends on the system’s energy and evolution time, the geometric phase is determined purely by the path traced in the Hilbert space. This unique property underpins the ‘all-geometric’ approach3,4, which serves as the foundation for fault-tolerant holonomic quantum computing5–14. Recently, classical wave systems—such as light and sound—with their rich and versatile degrees of freedom, have emerged as promising platforms for exploring non-Abelian geometric phases15–24. In this context, the ‘all-geometric-phase’ approach offers advantages including broad operational bandwidth and enhanced fabrication tolerance in optical computing applications24. However, the robustness that makes geometric phases appealing but also introduces a fundamental challenge: it inherently limits their tunability. The reported scheme for high-dimensional special-orthogonal (SO) holonomy24 is predetermined and fixed after fabrication, which cannot fulfill the requirements of programmable photonic circuits. Although the reconfigurable non-Abelian geometric phase has been demonstrated using the thermo-optic effect25, this implementation is limited to the braid group operations. While this scheme has potential for specialized tasks26, it falls short of enabling general-purpose photonic matrix computation. Therefore, realizing tunable non-Abelian holonomy over the full SO(m) group—combining the dynamic reconfigurability and the robustness of holonomy—is essential to support in-situ training27 and diverse computing tasks.

To realize the tunable non-Abelian geometric phase, a large refractive index modulation in the waveguide is necessary to manipulate the degenerate subspace. Conventional tuning mechanisms—such as the thermo-optic effect, free carrier dispersion effect, or Pockels effect28—typically induce only small changes in the refractive index. In contrast, chalcogenide phase change materials (PCMs) exhibit dramatic refractive index change during phase transitions, exceeding the tuning strength of conventional methods by 1 to 2 orders of magnitude29. Crucially, the optical states of PCMs are non-volatile, enabling lower energy consumption and in-memory storage of tuning states. The phase transition of PCMs is thermally driven and can be triggered by a laser within the PCM’s absorption band. A variety of applications have been demonstrated, including nonvolatile optical switching30–35, photonic memory36,37, analog-to-digital converter38, and in-memory photonic computing39–45. The low-loss PCMs, exemplified by Sb₂Se₃46, have enabled functionalities beyond memories47, such as post-fabrication tuning48, non-volatile tunable filtering49, and power splitting50,51. Combined with the simplicity of laser-driven reconfiguration, low-loss PCMs enable a powerful platform for investigating advanced physical mechanisms with flexible reconfigurability, including the tuning of non-Abelian geometric phases. The large refractive index contrast of PCMs enables complete and stable switching of holonomic evolution paths. Moreover, unlike thermally tuned approaches, PCM-based tuning is free of thermal crosstalk, allowing for independent control of individual waveguides and effectively avoiding degeneracy breaking caused by thermal-crosstalk induced refractive index perturbations.

In this work, we demonstrate tunable generic SO holonomy based on a three-layer photonic platform incorporating PCM waveguides, specifically utilizing Sb₂Se₃52. Some waveguides are made of Sb₂Se₃, while others are made of silicon. By switching the Sb₂Se₃ waveguide between its crystalline and amorphous states, the dimensionality of the degenerate subspace alternates between two and three, resulting in different holonomic paths and the enclosed solid angles. As a result, we achieve reconfigurable geometric operations of generic SO(2) transformations. Furthermore, multi-level tunability is available through the cascading of a series of basic SO(2) transformation components. For higher-dimensional matrices, an 8-level reconfigurable SO(3) transformation is synthesized by Givens rotations. Moreover, the proposed architecture supports high-dimensional non-Abelian braiding, which can be harnessed to construct scalable optical switch meshes. Figure 1a shows the conceptual illustration of tunable generic SO holonomies on a multilayer, heterogeneous photonic integration platform incorporating PCM, along with its potential applications in classical neuromorphic computing and holonomic quantum computing. Our work provides a promising pathway toward practical implementations of non-Abelian geometric phase in integrated photonics.

---

## Results

Tunable SO(2) holonomy
We implement the tunable non-Abelian holonomy in a three-layer heterogeneous integrated photonic platform incorporating PCM. As shown in Fig. 1b, all waveguides share an identical cross-section. The top waveguide is made of Sb₂Se₃, while the remaining waveguides are made of amorphous silicon. The inset in Fig. 1b shows the focused ion beam (FIB) cross-sectional image of the fabricated device. The top Sb₂Se₃ waveguide is patterned by inductively coupled plasma reactive ion etching using a Cl₂/Ar gas mixture. We use silica as both a protective layer and a hard mask for patterning. Figure 1c,d show the FIB images of a single Sb₂Se₃ waveguide fabricated on the substrate, confirming the quality of the Sb₂Se₃ waveguide. For the two-layer silicon waveguides, the scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images are provided in the Supplementary Figs. 8–10. The detailed fabrication process can be found in Methods and Supplementary Fig. 1.

The Hamiltonian of this five-waveguide system can be written as:

H(z) = \begin{pmatrix} \beta & \kappa_{AX}(z) & \kappa_{BX}(z) & \kappa_{CX}(z) & \kappa_{DX}(z) \\ \kappa_{AX}(z) & \beta & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ \kappa_{BX}(z) & 0 & \beta & 0 & 0 \\ \kappa_{CX}(z) & 0 & 0 & \beta & 0 \\ \kappa_{DX}(z) & 0 & 0 & 0 & \beta_P \end{pmatrix} (1)

Where β is the effective index of the individual silicon waveguides A, B, C, and X, where β_P is the effective index of the Sb₂Se₃ waveguide D. κ_{iX} (i=A, B, C, and D) represents the coupling coefficient between the surrounding waveguide i and the central waveguide X. Among these, κ_{AX} and κ_{DX} are fixed throughout the evolution, while κ_{BX} and κ_{CX} evolve adiabatically and are modulated by the gap distance. The number of degenerate states supported by this Hamiltonian can be actively controlled by switching the phase state of the Sb₂Se₃ waveguide. When Sb₂Se₃ is in the crystalline phase (Phase 1 in Fig. 1b), this Hamiltonian supports two degenerate states, as a result of the significant refractive index mismatch between crystalline Sb₂Se₃ and amorphous silicon (Supplementary Fig. 5, resulting in β ≠ β_P). As derived in Eqs. S2–S7, these two degenerate states (|D_1〉 and |D_2〉) can be utilized to construct an SO(2) holonomy20,21,24. When light is injected from waveguides B and C, the state lying in the degenerate subspace |ϕ(z)〉 = a_1(z)|D_1〉 + a_2(z)|D_2〉 is excited, and evolves under an SO(2) transformation e^{iθσ_y} (σ_y is the Pauli matrix53). θ is the solid angle enclosed by the holonomic path in the parameter space spanned by κ_{AX}, κ_{BX}, and κ_{CX}. In contrast, when Sb₂Se₃ transitions to its amorphous phase (Phase 2 in Fig. 1b), three degenerate states are preserved by chiral symmetry54 due to the refractive index matching between amorphous Sb₂Se₃ and amorphous silicon (Supplementary Fig. 5, resulting in β = β_P). As derived in Eqs. S11-S15, three degenerate states (|D_1〉, |D_2〉, and |D_3〉) form an SO(3) holonomy, with the Berry-Wilczek-Zee (BWZ) connection elements A_{3i} = A_{i3} = 0 (i=1, 2, 3) due to the fixed κ_{AX} and κ_{DX} throughout the evolution. When light is injected from waveguides B and C, only |D_1〉 and |D_2〉 are excited. The resulting evolution in the degenerate subspace spanned by |D_1〉 and |D_2〉 corresponds to an SO(2) rotation generated by σ_y which is a subgroup of the full SO(3) holonomy. But the accumulated geometric phase α differs from the phase θ observed in Phase 1 since it involves the participation of κ_{DX} (detailed in η and η’ of Eq. S7 and Eq. S14), and the control manifold is redefined as κ = \sqrt{κ_{AX}^2 + κ_{DX}^2}, κ_{BX}, κ_{CX}. Thus, the value of κ_{DX} and κ_{AX} determines the contrast of θ and α of this two-level tunable geometric phase.

Supplementary Fig. 3 illustrates an example of the two-level tunable SO(2) holonomy. Supplementary Fig. 3d simulates the optical evolution in Phase 1, where light remains confined to waveguides A, B, and C throughout the process, while waveguide D is decoupled from the degenerate space. In contrast, in Phase 2 (Supplementary Fig. 3e), waveguide D actively participates in the evolution of the degenerate space and significantly influence the final results of the SO(2) transformation compared to Phase 1 (Supplementary Fig. 3d). More information about the numerical simulation methods is provided in Methods.

To demonstrate the wide-range tunability of the system, we further propose a reconfigurable braiding protocol in which the geometric phase can be modulated between π/2 and 0. As illustrated in Fig. 1e, the structure incorporates three stimulated Raman adiabatic passage (STIRAP)55–59 processes, with the configuration parameters set as κ_{DX} ≫ κ_{AX}, κ_{BX} and κ_{CX}, enabling a wide-range tunability. When waveguide D is in Phase 1 (refractive index mismatched), it becomes decoupled from the degenerate space, enabling two-mode braiding16,18,23. In this scenario, the simulation results of the fundamental building blocks—namely, the lateral and vertical STIRAP processes—are shown in Supplementary Fig. 2a and 2c, respectively. As expected, when the input light excites the zero mode, the output exhibits a complete power swap. In contrast, when waveguide D transitions to Phase 2, where the refractive indices across all waveguides are matched, the configuration (κ_{DX} ≫ κ_{AX}, κ_{BX}, and κ_{CX}) leads to a complete power swap, as displayed in Supplementary Fig. 2b and 2d. The corresponding simulation confirms that the light remains localized in the input waveguide throughout the evolution, indicating the absence of any nontrivial SO(2) geometric phase.

In practical device models, certain factors may affect the degeneracy, such as the next-nearest-neighbor coupling coefficients60. Supplementary Fig. 14b-c presents the simulated next-nearest-neighbor coupling coefficients, which are approximately an order of magnitude smaller than the nearest-neighbor couplings. Supplementary Fig. 14f-g compares the optical evolution of a holonomy with (dashed lines) and without (solid lines) next-nearest-neighbor coupling. The agreement between the two cases indicates that next-nearest-neighbor coupling has a minimal impact on the holonomy process. To further account for all potential factors that may affect the degeneracy, we performed full-vectorial electromagnetic eigenmode simulations of the five-waveguide system using the commercial software Ansys Lumerical. Supplementary Fig. 7a-b illustrates the calculated effective indices of the five eigenmodes as a function of waveguide gap distance for both amorphous and crystalline PCM states. Threefold and twofold degeneracy are well preserved across most gap distances, except for a slight splitting observed at small gap distances. Therefore, the designed holonomic path should avoid these narrow-gap regimes. More details are provided in Supplementary Note 2.

Figure 2c presents the experimental results of a two-level tunable SO(2) holonomy. The light input/output from waveguides B and C excites the state within twofold degenerate subspace, which undergoes an SO(2) transformation. The measured intensities correspond to the absolute square of the matrix elements of the SO(2) transformation. The gap distances and the corresponding coupling coefficients between waveguides throughout the evolution are detailed in Supplementary Fig. 4a. By switching the phase state of the Sb₂Se₃ waveguide, the holonomic path traverses distinct degenerate subspaces, enabling the realization of different SO(2) holonomies. The holonomic paths in parameter space, along with the enclosed solid angles of the two phase states, are shown in Supplementary Fig. 4b-c. The conformity between theoretical prediction and experimental results is evaluated as fidelity; the fidelity of Phase 1 is 0.9991, and the fidelity of Phase 2 is 0.9993. The fidelity is defined as F=(1/N)|Tr(U_t^† U_{exp})|61–64 based on the Frobenius inner product, Tr(A) represents the trace of A, N is the dimension of the unitary matrix, U_t, U_{exp} are the theoretical and experimental unitary matrices, respectively. The phase transition of the Sb₂Se₃ waveguide between its crystalline and amorphous states can be achieved via laser direct-writing techniques, as the Sb₂Se₃ waveguide is located on the top layer of the device.

Figure 2d shows the experimental implementation of tunable two-mode braiding. The phase state of the Sb₂Se₃ waveguide determines whether the transformation corresponds to a ‘swap’ or ‘non-swap’ operation in the resulting matrix. The gap distances, coupling coefficients, and holonomic paths can be found in Supplementary Fig. 6. To demonstrate multi-level discrete reconfigurability, Fig. 2e illustrates the cascading of two independently tunable SO(2) building blocks. The detailed information is shown in Supplementary Fig. 3a–c. By adjusting the phase states of each unit, a composite transformation with multi-level tunability is achieved. As a proof of concept, we demonstrate three discrete geometric phase levels by cascading two identical building blocks. By employing non-identical units, the number of achievable levels can be expanded. In general, cascading n distinct units enables 2^n (n bits) discrete phase levels. Here, we propose a scalable scheme for generating equidistant geometric phases, as shown in Supplementary Fig. 11.

For the modulation of the phase states of Sb₂Se₃, Fig. 2a displays the microscope images of the reversible switching of the Sb₂Se₃ thin film, as well as the laser direct writing setup. We started with a crystalline Sb₂Se₃ film sandwiched between μm-thick SiO₂ layers on the Si substrate, and the crystallization state was obtained by thermally annealing the as-deposited amorphous film. A rectangular area was amorphized using 408-nm laser pulses from a commercial laser writing system. The grain texture of the pristine substrate transitioned to a smooth morphology in the written region, which suggested that the Sb₂Se₃ was laser-induced melted and rapidly quenched into a disordered glassy state. Simultaneously, the refractive index change of Sb₂Se₃ caused a distinct color change in the written area. The amorphization process was confirmed by the Raman spectra in Fig. 2b. The black curve shows the Raman spectrum of the crystalline Sb₂Se₃ thin film, where three characteristic peaks at 190 cm⁻¹ (A_g mode of Sb–Se bonds), 150 cm⁻¹ (B_g mode of Sb–Sb bonds), and 120 cm⁻¹ (A_g mode of Se–Se bonds)46,65–67 could be observed. The blue curve shows the Raman spectrum of the laser-switched area, where a broad peak centered around 190 cm⁻¹ stands for the amorphous feature65. Amorphous patterns on the crystalline substrate can be erased via annealing or laser pulses, which induce the recrystallization of amorphous Sb₂Se₃. During annealing, grains tend to start growing from the boundary between the amorphous and crystalline regions. Recrystallization of amorphous Sb₂Se₃ can also be achieved using our home-built 639-nm laser direct-writing system, where the laser scanning direction can form larger grains and guide the grain growth orientation to some extent. This creates granular contrasts between the recrystallized region and the original crystalline substrate, as seen in Fig. 2a. The Raman spectroscopy confirmed the laser-induced crystallization of an amorphous Sb₂Se₃ film, as indicated by the orange curve in Fig. 2b (the Raman intensity has been normalized), and the micro-area X-ray Diffraction (Micro-XRD) pattern further confirmed the lattice structure (as shown in Supplementary Fig. 12). More details are provided in Methods. Furthermore, to verify that our tuning method can achieve complete phase transition across the full thickness of the 100 nm-thick PCM layer, we conducted transmission electron microscopy (TEM, Talos F200X G2, Thermo Fisher Scientific) tests, which are discussed in Supplementary Note 3 and illustrated in Supplementary Fig. 13. The TEM and FFT analyses indicate that the 100 nm thin film exhibits no significant inhomogeneity or morphological differences between the upper and lower sections after laser-controlled phase transition switching. This suggests that the phase switching occurs throughout the entire thickness direction.

Tunable high-dimensional holonomy
To demonstrate the scalability of the architecture, a high-dimensional reconfigurable mesh is presented in Fig. 3. A 3-bit (8-level) tunable SO(3) transformation is implemented using the framework of Givens rotations. By selectively switching the phase state of each Sb₂Se₃ waveguide—either through laser direct-writing to induce the amorphous state or erasing to restore the crystalline state—we systematically measure all eight levels of the SO(3) holonomy. Figure 3a–c presents microscope images of laser direct writing on Sb₂Se₃ waveguides. Distinct textural differences are evident in the Sb₂Se₃ waveguides when comparing the crystalline and amorphous phases (e.g., Fig. 3a). Besides, due to the wider laser-written patterns compared to the Sb₂Se₃ waveguide width, the color contrast between the crystalline and amorphous regions can be clearly observed in the surrounding film areas. The corresponding mathematical models, experimentally measured matrix elements, and transformation fidelity for the 8-level SO(3) holonomy are also summarized in Fig. 3d–k. The presented magnitude corresponds to the absolute value of the matrix elements of the SO(3) transformation. The relatively high fidelity (>0.96) demonstrates the excellent repeatability of the cyclic erasing and writing process.

Figure 4 presents the experimental realization of reconfigurable three-mode braiding. Building upon the tunable two-mode braiding demonstrated in Fig. 2d, high-dimensional braiding can be constructed by assembling a scalable mesh through parallel and cascaded integration of the basic two-mode braiding unit. We experimentally demonstrate four representative three-mode braiding scenarios through three braiding devices, with corresponding theoretical models and measured intensity distributions shown in the figures. This approach offers a promising route toward large-scale, programmable optical switching and topological photonic circuits.

## Methods

Fabrication process
The fabrication process of the device is compatible with CMOS technology. The devices were fabricated on a 500-μm-thick silicon substrate wafer with a 3-μm-thick buried oxide layer. For the first layer, a 100-nm-thick amorphous silicon thin film was deposited by plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition (PECVD, Oxford Instruments). The PECVD gas included SiH_4 and Ar. Then, photoresist (AR-P 6200.09) was spun at a speed of 4000 r/min to have a thickness of 200 nm on the chip, and baked at a temperature of 180 °C for 2 min. The designed patterns were defined by electronic beam lithography (EBL, Vistec EBPG-5200), and the developing used methyl isobutyl ketone (MIBK, developing for 75 s) and isopropanol (IPA, developing for 60 s). Then it was fully etched through an inductively coupled plasma deep reactive ion etching system for silicon (ICP Deep RIE, SPTS Technologies). After that, the chip was coated with silica as the inter-layer dielectric using PECVD, and the chemical–mechanical polishing (CMP) was employed to planarize the silica. For the second layer, similar processes were repeated as the first layer, such as depositing a 100-nm-thick amorphous silicon film, defining patterns through EBL, fully ICP Deep RIE, PECVD, etc. For the patterning of the third-layer Sb₂Se₃ waveguides, we first deposited a 100-nm-thick Sb₂Se₃ film using magnetron sputtering (Denton). Subsequently, a 200-nm-thick silica protective layer was deposited using inductively coupled plasma chemical vapor deposition (ICPCVD, Oxford Instruments). Next, EBL and development were performed to define the waveguide pattern. This was followed by ICP etching of the silica protective layer, and finally, the Sb₂Se₃ film was etched by ICP reactive ion etching (Sentech) using a Cl₂/Ar gas mixture. The scanning electron microscope (SEM) figures and focused ion beam (FIB) images of the fabricated Sb₂Se₃ waveguides are provided in Fig. 1c,d. Finally, a 1-μm-thick silica cladding was deposited through ICPCVD. The fabrication process is summarized in Supplementary Fig. 1.

Measurement setup
The light is emitted from a wideband source (Wuhan Leicheng Photonics Technology Co., Ltd.), which covers a wavelength range of 1150–1680 nm. Then it propagates through a polarization controller and is coupled in/out to the integrated photonic chip. Edge couplers are utilized to interface the light between a single-mode fiber and a silicon waveguide. The light output is monitored by a power meter (JW3216, Shanghai Joinwit), and the spectra are analyzed through OSA (AQ6370C, YOKOGAWA).

Phase transition control of Sb₂Se₃
The transition from the crystalline to the amorphous phase is achieved via laser direct writing using a DWL 66+ system (Heidelberg Instruments) with a nominal laser power of 15 mW and a writing speed of 3 mm²/min. The transition from amorphous state to crystalline state can be realized through annealing (whole chip erasing, 200 °C, 5 min) or through laser-diode-writting (locally erasing) at a wavelength of 639 nm. Figure 2a illustrates the setup. Laser-diode-induced crystallization can be achieved using two distinct modes: (1) a continuous scanning mode with a laser power of 40 mW, a scanning speed of 0.01 mm/s, and an energy density of ~80 μJ/μm² on the sample surface; and (2) a single-pulse mode with a laser power of 6.95 mW, a pulse duration of 300 ms, and the same energy density of ~89 μJ/μm². To calibrate the time and energy needed for laser-controlled amorphization, amorphization was also demonstrated on this system using a single pulse with a power of 44 mW, a duration of 200 ns, and an energy density of ~5.7 nJ/μm².

Numerical simulation
We employ multiple simulation approaches for cross-validation. For the numerical calculation, one method involves computing the Wilczek–Zee connection integral using MATLAB. The other method is based on solving the Schrödinger-like equation i∂|φ(z)〉/∂z = Ĥ(z)|φ(z)〉 via the transfer matrix method, also implemented in MATLAB. These two methods fit well with each other. For the actual device simulation, a 3D finite-difference time-domain (3D-FDTD) full-wave simulation for the electromagnetic field is utilized through commercial software Lumerical. The coupling coefficients between two identical waveguides are calculated through Mode solutions that κ = (n_s - n_a)/2 75, where n_s, n_a are effective index of symmetric and anti-symmetric supermodes, respectively. The results from the numerical calculation and actual device simulation are also in close agreement.

Data availability
The source data generated in this study are available in the Figshare repository https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.30876017. Source data are provided with this paper.

## Your Original Review (Round 1)

### Reviewer 1

The control of holonomy has recently emerged as a highly active topic, attracting broad interest across various physical disciplines. In this context, the manuscript entitled “In-memory multilevel control of generic SO(m) holonomy in photonics” by Chen et al. presents a novel approach to implementing nonvolatile and tunable holonomic control by manipulating degenerate photonic states. Specifically, the authors cleverly introduce a five-waveguide architecture incorporating a phase-change material (PCM) waveguide, which enables the realization of two- and three-fold degeneracies. This in turn allows for the demonstration of fundamental SO(2) holonomic transformations, as well as the prospect of extending to in-memory, multilevel control of higher-dimensional SO(m) holonomies through cascaded designs. The proposed scheme is original and timely, offering a potentially significant contribution to both the fundamental study of non-Abelian photonics and the development of reconfigurable photonic devices. Since this work represents a big advance that is likely to stimulate further research in this area, I would support the publication of the manuscript after the authors address my following comments.
1. Please clarify whether the targeted degeneracies are well preserved in both the amorphous and crystalline states of the five-waveguide system. Since the presence of multiple coupled waveguides can sometimes introduce unwanted perturbations that affect the robustness of degeneracy (see, for example, Phys. Rev. A 105, 013507 (2021)), a more detailed analysis would strengthen the work. In particular, simulations of the effective indices of the five modes as a function of gap distance in the actual device model could help demonstrate that the two- or three-fold degeneracies remain well preserved across both material states. Besides, the detailed parameters of reconfigurable two-mode braiding, including the evolution of gap distances, coupling coefficients, and holonomic path, should be provided.
2. Regarding fabrication, Supplementary Fig. 1 and the Methods section do not mention any planarization steps. Since multilayer structures, particularly those involving braiding, typically require good planarity, it would be useful to clarify whether a planarization process (e.g., chemical–mechanical polishing) was employed. For the PCM integration, the manuscript presents SEM images of Sb₂Se₃ waveguides, but not of the silicon waveguides used in the holonomy structures. Providing SEM figures of the silicon waveguides would improve the completeness of the work. In addition, while PCM layers in photonic devices are often on the order of tens of nanometers, the PCM waveguide here is significantly thicker. Given the limited penetration depth of visible laser light in PCM, this could lead to non-uniform phase transitions and refractive index gradients along the thickness direction after laser writing. A discussion on how such effects may influence the reversibility of laser switching and the stability of reconfigurable geometric phases would further strengthen the work.
3. For the in-memory reconfiguration of SO(m) holonomy, two laser direct writing systems operating at 408 nm and 639 nm were employed for amorphization and crystallization of the PCM, respectively. Why are two distinct laser systems used? Also, the parameters of the specific control pulse for the phase switching process should be provided in detail. Further, the laser-triggered phase transition in Sb2Se3 is characterized by grain morphology under microscopy and Raman spectroscopy. While X-ray diffraction analysis would offer more direct observation of the lattice structure changes through diffraction peaks, I would suggest the authors to add XRD results as Supplementary data.

It would be interesting to discuss how the system behaves when the PCM is in intermediate states (see, e.g., Nat. Commun. 15, 2786 (2024)), as this may introduce additional levels of control. Furthermore, the current design assumes a uniform phase change across the entire waveguide. Considering the case where only a portion of the waveguide undergoes a phase transition may open the possibility of generating multiple geometric-phase levels within a single device. A discussion along these lines would strengthen the manuscript by highlighting the broader tunability and versatility of the proposed approach.
5. For the multilevel control of SO(2) holonomy, the authors demonstrate three discrete levels by cascading two identical building blocks. While this provides a useful proof of concept, the scheme could potentially be extended further for a more insightful discussion. In particular, cascading non-identical building blocks may enable a richer set of discrete levels and more versatile control.

### Reviewer 2

This work demonstrates in-memory multilevel control of generic SO(m) holonomy using a multilayer silicon photonic platform integrated with the phase-change material Sb₂Se₃. By optically switching the Sb₂Se₃ waveguides between amorphous and crystalline states, the authors dynamically modulate the number of degenerate modes in the system, enabling reconfigurable non-Abelian geometric phases without volatile external controls. They experimentally achieve high-fidelity, nonvolatile SO(2) and SO(3) transformations, along with tunable two- and three-mode braiding operations, and showcase multi-level programmability through cascaded SO(2) units and Givens rotations. This approach merges the inherent robustness of geometric phases with the nonvolatile tunability of PCMs, offering a promising pathway toward fault-tolerant photonic quantum processing, reconfigurable optical switching networks, and high-dimensional classical neuromorphic computing.
In my opinions, this work demonstrates the first experimental realization of reconfigurable control over non-Abelian holonomy, which exhibits notable innovation. However, several issues should be addressed prior to publication:
1. First and foremost, regarding novelty, this work combines the concepts of "reconfigurability" and "non-Abelian holonomy," which brings to mind two related works also published in Nature Communications: Nat. Commun. 16, 7089 (2025) and Nat. Commun. 16, 3650 (2025). Compared to the former, this study extends braiding operations to more general holonomic scenarios and introduces a new refractive index tuning method; compared to the latter, it achieves dynamic control over the SO(m) group. The authors should provide more detailed and specific comparisons with these relevant works, and include necessary discussions in the manuscript to better highlight the originality and significance of their contribution.
2. As a follow-up to the point above, different to Nat. Commun. 16, 7089 (2025), which employs the thermo-optic effect for active tuning, this work utilizes the phase-change material, claiming advantages in lower energy consumption and improved stability. The authors are encouraged to provide a detailed comparison of the advantages and disadvantages of different active tuning methods to underscore the technical and systemic innovation of their approach.
3. While the active tuning strategy presented is appealing, it remains limited to switching between SO(2) and SO(3) based on the presence or absence of onsite index mismatch. It would be valuable if the authors could discuss whether their method can be extended to design more complex or interesting functionalities.
4. The caption of Figure 2e is overly brief. A more detailed explanation of how the SO(2) transformation is realized in parameter space should be provided to assist readers unfamiliar with the process of non-Abelian holonomy.
5. The multilayer quasi-3D waveguide platform constructed using deposited SiO₂ is a promising architecture. However, a valid concern is whether next-nearest-neighbor coupling coefficients (such as κCD) can be neglected in such multilayer waveguides, and whether they might disrupt the holonomy process. Supplementary data on coupling coefficients should be provided in the Supplementary Information of this work to facilitate reader understanding.
6. Several minor issues require attention: the parameter space vectors on lines 91 and 136 contain a square symbol on the left-hand side of the equation, which may be a display error. The matrix alignment in Eq. (1) is also irregular. The authors should correct these and carefully check for other similar issues throughout the text.

(i) Compared with the reconfigurable braiding [Nat. Commun. 16, 7089 (2025)].
The first distinction lies in the theoretical mechanism. As illustrated in Fig. R12,
[Nat. Commun. 16, 7089 (2025)] employ a four-waveguide structure that supports
two degenerate modes for braiding in the absence of heating. Upon applying heat to
modulate the refractive index of waveguides, chiral symmetry of the Hamiltonian is
broken, causing the eigenmodes to localize at the input waveguides of each STIRAP
channel, and it’s notable that the degeneracy is lifted off in the meantime. In contrast,
our scheme is based on directly manipulating the dimensionality of degenerate
subspaces. The five-waveguide structure supports either a two-fold or three-fold
degenerate states, enabling a switchable holonomic path in different degenerate
subspaces. Thus, both states are based on geometric phase.
The second distinction lies in the tuning range. [Nat. Commun. 16, 7089 (2025)]
achieves reconfigurability within braid groups. In contrast, our system enables control
over the SO(2) group, which is further expanded to the control of SO(m) by Givens
rotations.
The third distinction lies in the tuning methods, [Nat. Commun. 16, 7089 (2025)]
utilizes the thermo-optics effect to modulate the effective index of waveguides. Our
work uses phase-change material (PCM) as the active in-memory manipulation
method. PCM has the advantages of large-index-contrast, zero static-power
consumption, and zero thermal crosstalk, which we will discuss in detail in the next
response.

## Paper

## Abstract

Non-Abelian geometric phases offer fault-tolerant unitary operations that are essential for holonomic quantum computation. While the “all-geometric” approach has successfully enabled robust control of atoms, ions, and electrons in various quantum systems, its photonic implementations have remained limited by a lack of tunability—an essential feature for modern classical or quantum optical information processing. Here, we demonstrate non-volatile multilevel tunable generic special-orthogonal (SO) geometric phases on a multilayer silicon photonic platform incorporating the phase-change material (PCM) of Sb₂Se₃. By toggling Sb₂Se₃ between crystalline and amorphous states, we dynamically control the number of degenerate states involved in the holonomy, enabling switching between different holonomic paths and SO(m) geometric transformations. Our results bridge the key gap between robust geometric-phase control and in-memory reconfigurable photonics, establishing a paradigm for fault-tolerant, high-dimensional operations in integrated optical systems.

---

## Introduction

The non-Abelian geometric phase is well known for its inherent robustness in realizing unitary transformations. Building upon the foundational work on the Berry phase1, Wilczek and Zee pointed out that a matrix-valued geometric phase can emerge from the adiabatic evolution of degenerate quantum states2. Unlike the dynamic phase, which depends on the system’s energy and evolution time, the geometric phase is determined purely by the path traced in the Hilbert space. This unique property underpins the ‘all-geometric’ approach3,4, which serves as the foundation for fault-tolerant holonomic quantum computing5–14. Recently, classical wave systems—such as light and sound—with their rich and versatile degrees of freedom, have emerged as promising platforms for exploring non-Abelian geometric phases15–24. In this context, the ‘all-geometric-phase’ approach offers advantages including broad operational bandwidth and enhanced fabrication tolerance in optical computing applications24. However, the robustness that makes geometric phases appealing but also introduces a fundamental challenge: it inherently limits their tunability. The reported scheme for high-dimensional special-orthogonal (SO) holonomy24 is predetermined and fixed after fabrication, which cannot fulfill the requirements of programmable photonic circuits. Although the reconfigurable non-Abelian geometric phase has been demonstrated using the thermo-optic effect25, this implementation is limited to the braid group operations. While this scheme has potential for specialized tasks26, it falls short of enabling general-purpose photonic matrix computation. Therefore, realizing tunable non-Abelian holonomy over the full SO(m) group—combining the dynamic reconfigurability and the robustness of holonomy—is essential to support in-situ training27 and diverse computing tasks.

To realize the tunable non-Abelian geometric phase, a large refractive index modulation in the waveguide is necessary to manipulate the degenerate subspace. Conventional tuning mechanisms—such as the thermo-optic effect, free carrier dispersion effect, or Pockels effect28—typically induce only small changes in the refractive index. In contrast, chalcogenide phase change materials (PCMs) exhibit dramatic refractive index change during phase transitions, exceeding the tuning strength of conventional methods by 1 to 2 orders of magnitude29. Crucially, the optical states of PCMs are non-volatile, enabling lower energy consumption and in-memory storage of tuning states. The phase transition of PCMs is thermally driven and can be triggered by a laser within the PCM’s absorption band. A variety of applications have been demonstrated, including nonvolatile optical switching30–35, photonic memory36,37, analog-to-digital converter38, and in-memory photonic computing39–45. The low-loss PCMs, exemplified by Sb₂Se₃46, have enabled functionalities beyond memories47, such as post-fabrication tuning48, non-volatile tunable filtering49, and power splitting50,51. Combined with the simplicity of laser-driven reconfiguration, low-loss PCMs enable a powerful platform for investigating advanced physical mechanisms with flexible reconfigurability, including the tuning of non-Abelian geometric phases. The large refractive index contrast of PCMs enables complete and stable switching of holonomic evolution paths. Moreover, unlike thermally tuned approaches, PCM-based tuning is free of thermal crosstalk, allowing for independent control of individual waveguides and effectively avoiding degeneracy breaking caused by thermal-crosstalk induced refractive index perturbations.

In this work, we demonstrate tunable generic SO holonomy based on a three-layer photonic platform incorporating PCM waveguides, specifically utilizing Sb₂Se₃52. Some waveguides are made of Sb₂Se₃, while others are made of silicon. By switching the Sb₂Se₃ waveguide between its crystalline and amorphous states, the dimensionality of the degenerate subspace alternates between two and three, resulting in different holonomic paths and the enclosed solid angles. As a result, we achieve reconfigurable geometric operations of generic SO(2) transformations. Furthermore, multi-level tunability is available through the cascading of a series of basic SO(2) transformation components. For higher-dimensional matrices, an 8-level reconfigurable SO(3) transformation is synthesized by Givens rotations. Moreover, the proposed architecture supports high-dimensional non-Abelian braiding, which can be harnessed to construct scalable optical switch meshes. Figure 1a shows the conceptual illustration of tunable generic SO holonomies on a multilayer, heterogeneous photonic integration platform incorporating PCM, along with its potential applications in classical neuromorphic computing and holonomic quantum computing. Our work provides a promising pathway toward practical implementations of non-Abelian geometric phase in integrated photonics.

## Results

Tunable SO(2) holonomy
We implement the tunable non-Abelian holonomy in a three-layer heterogeneous integrated photonic platform incorporating PCM. As shown in Fig. 1b, all waveguides share an identical cross-section. The top waveguide is made of Sb₂Se₃, while the remaining waveguides are made of amorphous silicon. The inset in Fig. 1b shows the focused ion beam (FIB) cross-sectional image of the fabricated device. The top Sb₂Se₃ waveguide is patterned by inductively coupled plasma reactive ion etching using a Cl₂/Ar gas mixture. We use silica as both a protective layer and a hard mask for patterning. Figure 1c,d show the FIB images of a single Sb₂Se₃ waveguide fabricated on the substrate, confirming the quality of the Sb₂Se₃ waveguide. For the two-layer silicon waveguides, the scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images are provided in the Supplementary Figs. 8–10. The detailed fabrication process can be found in Methods and Supplementary Fig. 1.

The Hamiltonian of this five-waveguide system can be written as:

H(z) = \begin{pmatrix} \beta & \kappa_{AX}(z) & \kappa_{BX}(z) & \kappa_{CX}(z) & \kappa_{DX}(z) \\ \kappa_{AX}(z) & \beta & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ \kappa_{BX}(z) & 0 & \beta & 0 & 0 \\ \kappa_{CX}(z) & 0 & 0 & \beta & 0 \\ \kappa_{DX}(z) & 0 & 0 & 0 & \beta_P \end{pmatrix} (1)

Where β is the effective index of the individual silicon waveguides A, B, C, and X, where β_P is the effective index of the Sb₂Se₃ waveguide D. κ_{iX} (i=A, B, C, and D) represents the coupling coefficient between the surrounding waveguide i and the central waveguide X. Among these, κ_{AX} and κ_{DX} are fixed throughout the evolution, while κ_{BX} and κ_{CX} evolve adiabatically and are modulated by the gap distance. The number of degenerate states supported by this Hamiltonian can be actively controlled by switching the phase state of the Sb₂Se₃ waveguide. When Sb₂Se₃ is in the crystalline phase (Phase 1 in Fig. 1b), this Hamiltonian supports two degenerate states, as a result of the significant refractive index mismatch between crystalline Sb₂Se₃ and amorphous silicon (Supplementary Fig. 5, resulting in β ≠ β_P). As derived in Eqs. S2–S7, these two degenerate states (|D_1〉 and |D_2〉) can be utilized to construct an SO(2) holonomy20,21,24. When light is injected from waveguides B and C, the state lying in the degenerate subspace |ϕ(z)〉 = a_1(z)|D_1〉 + a_2(z)|D_2〉 is excited, and evolves under an SO(2) transformation e^{iθσ_y} (σ_y is the Pauli matrix53). θ is the solid angle enclosed by the holonomic path in the parameter space spanned by κ_{AX}, κ_{BX}, and κ_{CX}. In contrast, when Sb₂Se₃ transitions to its amorphous phase (Phase 2 in Fig. 1b), three degenerate states are preserved by chiral symmetry54 due to the refractive index matching between amorphous Sb₂Se₃ and amorphous silicon (Supplementary Fig. 5, resulting in β = β_P). As derived in Eqs. S11-S15, three degenerate states (|D_1〉, |D_2〉, and |D_3〉) form an SO(3) holonomy, with the Berry-Wilczek-Zee (BWZ) connection elements A_{3i} = A_{i3} = 0 (i=1, 2, 3) due to the fixed κ_{AX} and κ_{DX} throughout the evolution. When light is injected from waveguides B and C, only |D_1〉 and |D_2〉 are excited. The resulting evolution in the degenerate subspace spanned by |D_1〉 and |D_2〉 corresponds to an SO(2) rotation generated by σ_y which is a subgroup of the full SO(3) holonomy. But the accumulated geometric phase α differs from the phase θ observed in Phase 1 since it involves the participation of κ_{DX} (detailed in η and η’ of Eq. S7 and Eq. S14), and the control manifold is redefined as κ = \sqrt{κ_{AX}^2 + κ_{DX}^2}, κ_{BX}, κ_{CX}. Thus, the value of κ_{DX} and κ_{AX} determines the contrast of θ and α of this two-level tunable geometric phase.

Supplementary Fig. 3 illustrates an example of the two-level tunable SO(2) holonomy. Supplementary Fig. 3d simulates the optical evolution in Phase 1, where light remains confined to waveguides A, B, and C throughout the process, while waveguide D is decoupled from the degenerate space. In contrast, in Phase 2 (Supplementary Fig. 3e), waveguide D actively participates in the evolution of the degenerate space and significantly influence the final results of the SO(2) transformation compared to Phase 1 (Supplementary Fig. 3d). More information about the numerical simulation methods is provided in Methods.

To demonstrate the wide-range tunability of the system, we further propose a reconfigurable braiding protocol in which the geometric phase can be modulated between π/2 and 0. As illustrated in Fig. 1e, the structure incorporates three stimulated Raman adiabatic passage (STIRAP)55–59 processes, with the configuration parameters set as κ_{DX} ≫ κ_{AX}, κ_{BX} and κ_{CX}, enabling a wide-range tunability. When waveguide D is in Phase 1 (refractive index mismatched), it becomes decoupled from the degenerate space, enabling two-mode braiding16,18,23. In this scenario, the simulation results of the fundamental building blocks—namely, the lateral and vertical STIRAP processes—are shown in Supplementary Fig. 2a and 2c, respectively. As expected, when the input light excites the zero mode, the output exhibits a complete power swap. In contrast, when waveguide D transitions to Phase 2, where the refractive indices across all waveguides are matched, the configuration (κ_{DX} ≫ κ_{AX}, κ_{BX}, and κ_{CX}) leads to a complete power swap, as displayed in Supplementary Fig. 2b and 2d. The corresponding simulation confirms that the light remains localized in the input waveguide throughout the evolution, indicating the absence of any nontrivial SO(2) geometric phase.

In practical device models, certain factors may affect the degeneracy, such as the next-nearest-neighbor coupling coefficients60. Supplementary Fig. 14b-c presents the simulated next-nearest-neighbor coupling coefficients, which are approximately an order of magnitude smaller than the nearest-neighbor couplings. Supplementary Fig. 14f-g compares the optical evolution of a holonomy with (dashed lines) and without (solid lines) next-nearest-neighbor coupling. The agreement between the two cases indicates that next-nearest-neighbor coupling has a minimal impact on the holonomy process. To further account for all potential factors that may affect the degeneracy, we performed full-vectorial electromagnetic eigenmode simulations of the five-waveguide system using the commercial software Ansys Lumerical. Supplementary Fig. 7a-b illustrates the calculated effective indices of the five eigenmodes as a function of waveguide gap distance for both amorphous and crystalline PCM states. Threefold and twofold degeneracy are well preserved across most gap distances, except for a slight splitting observed at small gap distances. Therefore, the designed holonomic path should avoid these narrow-gap regimes. More details are provided in Supplementary Note 2.

Figure 2c presents the experimental results of a two-level tunable SO(2) holonomy. The light input/output from waveguides B and C excites the state within twofold degenerate subspace, which undergoes an SO(2) transformation. The measured intensities correspond to the absolute square of the matrix elements of the SO(2) transformation. The gap distances and the corresponding coupling coefficients between waveguides throughout the evolution are detailed in Supplementary Fig. 4a. By switching the phase state of the Sb₂Se₃ waveguide, the holonomic path traverses distinct degenerate subspaces, enabling the realization of different SO(2) holonomies. The holonomic paths in parameter space, along with the enclosed solid angles of the two phase states, are shown in Supplementary Fig. 4b-c. The conformity between theoretical prediction and experimental results is evaluated as fidelity; the fidelity of Phase 1 is 0.9991, and the fidelity of Phase 2 is 0.9993. The fidelity is defined as F=(1/N)|Tr(U_t^† U_{exp})|61–64 based on the Frobenius inner product, Tr(A) represents the trace of A, N is the dimension of the unitary matrix, U_t, U_{exp} are the theoretical and experimental unitary matrices, respectively. The phase transition of the Sb₂Se₃ waveguide between its crystalline and amorphous states can be achieved via laser direct-writing techniques, as the Sb₂Se₃ waveguide is located on the top layer of the device.

Figure 2d shows the experimental implementation of tunable two-mode braiding. The phase state of the Sb₂Se₃ waveguide determines whether the transformation corresponds to a ‘swap’ or ‘non-swap’ operation in the resulting matrix. The gap distances, coupling coefficients, and holonomic paths can be found in Supplementary Fig. 6. To demonstrate multi-level discrete reconfigurability, Fig. 2e illustrates the cascading of two independently tunable SO(2) building blocks. The detailed information is shown in Supplementary Fig. 3a–c. By adjusting the phase states of each unit, a composite transformation with multi-level tunability is achieved. As a proof of concept, we demonstrate three discrete geometric phase levels by cascading two identical building blocks. By employing non-identical units, the number of achievable levels can be expanded. In general, cascading n distinct units enables 2^n (n bits) discrete phase levels. Here, we propose a scalable scheme for generating equidistant geometric phases, as shown in Supplementary Fig. 11.

For the modulation of the phase states of Sb₂Se₃, Fig. 2a displays the microscope images of the reversible switching of the Sb₂Se₃ thin film, as well as the laser direct writing setup. We started with a crystalline Sb₂Se₃ film sandwiched between μm-thick SiO₂ layers on the Si substrate, and the crystallization state was obtained by thermally annealing the as-deposited amorphous film. A rectangular area was amorphized using 408-nm laser pulses from a commercial laser writing system. The grain texture of the pristine substrate transitioned to a smooth morphology in the written region, which suggested that the Sb₂Se₃ was laser-induced melted and rapidly quenched into a disordered glassy state. Simultaneously, the refractive index change of Sb₂Se₃ caused a distinct color change in the written area. The amorphization process was confirmed by the Raman spectra in Fig. 2b. The black curve shows the Raman spectrum of the crystalline Sb₂Se₃ thin film, where three characteristic peaks at 190 cm⁻¹ (A_g mode of Sb–Se bonds), 150 cm⁻¹ (B_g mode of Sb–Sb bonds), and 120 cm⁻¹ (A_g mode of Se–Se bonds)46,65–67 could be observed. The blue curve shows the Raman spectrum of the laser-switched area, where a broad peak centered around 190 cm⁻¹ stands for the amorphous feature65. Amorphous patterns on the crystalline substrate can be erased via annealing or laser pulses, which induce the recrystallization of amorphous Sb₂Se₃. During annealing, grains tend to start growing from the boundary between the amorphous and crystalline regions. Recrystallization of amorphous Sb₂Se₃ can also be achieved using our home-built 639-nm laser direct-writing system, where the laser scanning direction can form larger grains and guide the grain growth orientation to some extent. This creates granular contrasts between the recrystallized region and the original crystalline substrate, as seen in Fig. 2a. The Raman spectroscopy confirmed the laser-induced crystallization of an amorphous Sb₂Se₃ film, as indicated by the orange curve in Fig. 2b (the Raman intensity has been normalized), and the micro-area X-ray Diffraction (Micro-XRD) pattern further confirmed the lattice structure (as shown in Supplementary Fig. 12). More details are provided in Methods. Furthermore, to verify that our tuning method can achieve complete phase transition across the full thickness of the 100 nm-thick PCM layer, we conducted transmission electron microscopy (TEM, Talos F200X G2, Thermo Fisher Scientific) tests, which are discussed in Supplementary Note 3 and illustrated in Supplementary Fig. 13. The TEM and FFT analyses indicate that the 100 nm thin film exhibits no significant inhomogeneity or morphological differences between the upper and lower sections after laser-controlled phase transition switching. This suggests that the phase switching occurs throughout the entire thickness direction.

Tunable high-dimensional holonomy
To demonstrate the scalability of the architecture, a high-dimensional reconfigurable mesh is presented in Fig. 3. A 3-bit (8-level) tunable SO(3) transformation is implemented using the framework of Givens rotations. By selectively switching the phase state of each Sb₂Se₃ waveguide—either through laser direct-writing to induce the amorphous state or erasing to restore the crystalline state—we systematically measure all eight levels of the SO(3) holonomy. Figure 3a–c presents microscope images of laser direct writing on Sb₂Se₃ waveguides. Distinct textural differences are evident in the Sb₂Se₃ waveguides when comparing the crystalline and amorphous phases (e.g., Fig. 3a). Besides, due to the wider laser-written patterns compared to the Sb₂Se₃ waveguide width, the color contrast between the crystalline and amorphous regions can be clearly observed in the surrounding film areas. The corresponding mathematical models, experimentally measured matrix elements, and transformation fidelity for the 8-level SO(3) holonomy are also summarized in Fig. 3d–k. The presented magnitude corresponds to the absolute value of the matrix elements of the SO(3) transformation. The relatively high fidelity (>0.96) demonstrates the excellent repeatability of the cyclic erasing and writing process.

Figure 4 presents the experimental realization of reconfigurable three-mode braiding. Building upon the tunable two-mode braiding demonstrated in Fig. 2d, high-dimensional braiding can be constructed by assembling a scalable mesh through parallel and cascaded integration of the basic two-mode braiding unit. We experimentally demonstrate four representative three-mode braiding scenarios through three braiding devices, with corresponding theoretical models and measured intensity distributions shown in the figures. This approach offers a promising route toward large-scale, programmable optical switching and topological photonic circuits.

## Methods

Fabrication process
The fabrication process of the device is compatible with CMOS technology. The devices were fabricated on a 500-μm-thick silicon substrate wafer with a 3-μm-thick buried oxide layer. For the first layer, a 100-nm-thick amorphous silicon thin film was deposited by plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition (PECVD, Oxford Instruments). The PECVD gas included SiH_4 and Ar. Then, photoresist (AR-P 6200.09) was spun at a speed of 4000 r/min to have a thickness of 200 nm on the chip, and baked at a temperature of 180 °C for 2 min. The designed patterns were defined by electronic beam lithography (EBL, Vistec EBPG-5200), and the developing used methyl isobutyl ketone (MIBK, developing for 75 s) and isopropanol (IPA, developing for 60 s). Then it was fully etched through an inductively coupled plasma deep reactive ion etching system for silicon (ICP Deep RIE, SPTS Technologies). After that, the chip was coated with silica as the inter-layer dielectric using PECVD, and the chemical–mechanical polishing (CMP) was employed to planarize the silica. For the second layer, similar processes were repeated as the first layer, such as depositing a 100-nm-thick amorphous silicon film, defining patterns through EBL, fully ICP Deep RIE, PECVD, etc. For the patterning of the third-layer Sb₂Se₃ waveguides, we first deposited a 100-nm-thick Sb₂Se₃ film using magnetron sputtering (Denton). Subsequently, a 200-nm-thick silica protective layer was deposited using inductively coupled plasma chemical vapor deposition (ICPCVD, Oxford Instruments). Next, EBL and development were performed to define the waveguide pattern. This was followed by ICP etching of the silica protective layer, and finally, the Sb₂Se₃ film was etched by ICP reactive ion etching (Sentech) using a Cl₂/Ar gas mixture. The scanning electron microscope (SEM) figures and focused ion beam (FIB) images of the fabricated Sb₂Se₃ waveguides are provided in Fig. 1c,d. Finally, a 1-μm-thick silica cladding was deposited through ICPCVD. The fabrication process is summarized in Supplementary Fig. 1.

Measurement setup
The light is emitted from a wideband source (Wuhan Leicheng Photonics Technology Co., Ltd.), which covers a wavelength range of 1150–1680 nm. Then it propagates through a polarization controller and is coupled in/out to the integrated photonic chip. Edge couplers are utilized to interface the light between a single-mode fiber and a silicon waveguide. The light output is monitored by a power meter (JW3216, Shanghai Joinwit), and the spectra are analyzed through OSA (AQ6370C, YOKOGAWA).

Phase transition control of Sb₂Se₃
The transition from the crystalline to the amorphous phase is achieved via laser direct writing using a DWL 66+ system (Heidelberg Instruments) with a nominal laser power of 15 mW and a writing speed of 3 mm²/min. The transition from amorphous state to crystalline state can be realized through annealing (whole chip erasing, 200 °C, 5 min) or through laser-diode-writting (locally erasing) at a wavelength of 639 nm. Figure 2a illustrates the setup. Laser-diode-induced crystallization can be achieved using two distinct modes: (1) a continuous scanning mode with a laser power of 40 mW, a scanning speed of 0.01 mm/s, and an energy density of ~80 μJ/μm² on the sample surface; and (2) a single-pulse mode with a laser power of 6.95 mW, a pulse duration of 300 ms, and the same energy density of ~89 μJ/μm². To calibrate the time and energy needed for laser-controlled amorphization, amorphization was also demonstrated on this system using a single pulse with a power of 44 mW, a duration of 200 ns, and an energy density of ~5.7 nJ/μm².

Numerical simulation
We employ multiple simulation approaches for cross-validation. For the numerical calculation, one method involves computing the Wilczek–Zee connection integral using MATLAB. The other method is based on solving the Schrödinger-like equation i∂|φ(z)〉/∂z = Ĥ(z)|φ(z)〉 via the transfer matrix method, also implemented in MATLAB. These two methods fit well with each other. For the actual device simulation, a 3D finite-difference time-domain (3D-FDTD) full-wave simulation for the electromagnetic field is utilized through commercial software Lumerical. The coupling coefficients between two identical waveguides are calculated through Mode solutions that κ = (n_s - n_a)/2 75, where n_s, n_a are effective index of symmetric and anti-symmetric supermodes, respectively. The results from the numerical calculation and actual device simulation are also in close agreement.

Data availability
The source data generated in this study are available in the Figshare repository https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.30876017. Source data are provided with this paper.

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

The control of holonomy has recently emerged as a highly active topic, attracting broad interest across various physical disciplines. In this context, the manuscript entitled “In-memory multilevel control of generic SO(m) holonomy in photonics” by Chen et al. presents a novel approach to implementing nonvolatile and tunable holonomic control by manipulating degenerate photonic states. Specifically, the authors cleverly introduce a five-waveguide architecture incorporating a phase-change material (PCM) waveguide, which enables the realization of two- and three-fold degeneracies. This in turn allows for the demonstration of fundamental SO(2) holonomic transformations, as well as the prospect of extending to in-memory, multilevel control of higher-dimensional SO(m) holonomies through cascaded designs. The proposed scheme is original and timely, offering a potentially significant contribution to both the fundamental study of non-Abelian photonics and the development of reconfigurable photonic devices. Since this work represents a big advance that is likely to stimulate further research in this area, I would support the publication of the manuscript after the authors address my following comments.
1. Please clarify whether the targeted degeneracies are well preserved in both the amorphous and crystalline states of the five-waveguide system. Since the presence of multiple coupled waveguides can sometimes introduce unwanted perturbations that affect the robustness of degeneracy (see, for example, Phys. Rev. A 105, 013507 (2021)), a more detailed analysis would strengthen the work. In particular, simulations of the effective indices of the five modes as a function of gap distance in the actual device model could help demonstrate that the two- or three-fold degeneracies remain well preserved across both material states. Besides, the detailed parameters of reconfigurable two-mode braiding, including the evolution of gap distances, coupling coefficients, and holonomic path, should be provided.
2. Regarding fabrication, Supplementary Fig. 1 and the Methods section do not mention any planarization steps. Since multilayer structures, particularly those involving braiding, typically require good planarity, it would be useful to clarify whether a planarization process (e.g., chemical–mechanical polishing) was employed. For the PCM integration, the manuscript presents SEM images of Sb₂Se₃ waveguides, but not of the silicon waveguides used in the holonomy structures. Providing SEM figures of the silicon waveguides would improve the completeness of the work. In addition, while PCM layers in photonic devices are often on the order of tens of nanometers, the PCM waveguide here is significantly thicker. Given the limited penetration depth of visible laser light in PCM, this could lead to non-uniform phase transitions and refractive index gradients along the thickness direction after laser writing. A discussion on how such effects may influence the reversibility of laser switching and the stability of reconfigurable geometric phases would further strengthen the work.
3. For the in-memory reconfiguration of SO(m) holonomy, two laser direct writing systems operating at 408 nm and 639 nm were employed for amorphization and crystallization of the PCM, respectively. Why are two distinct laser systems used? Also, the parameters of the specific control pulse for the phase switching process should be provided in detail. Further, the laser-triggered phase transition in Sb2Se3 is characterized by grain morphology under microscopy and Raman spectroscopy. While X-ray diffraction analysis would offer more direct observation of the lattice structure changes through diffraction peaks, I would suggest the authors to add XRD results as Supplementary data.
4. The demonstration of two-level SO(2) holonomy relies on the binary switching between the amorphous and crystalline states of the PCM. It would be interesting to discuss how the system behaves when the PCM is in intermediate states (see, e.g., Nat. Commun. 15, 2786 (2024)), as this may introduce additional levels of control. Furthermore, the current design assumes a uniform phase change across the entire waveguide. Considering the case where only a portion of the waveguide undergoes a phase transition may open the possibility of generating multiple geometric-phase levels within a single device. A discussion along these lines would strengthen the manuscript by highlighting the broader tunability and versatility of the proposed approach.
5. For the multilevel control of SO(2) holonomy, the authors demonstrate three discrete levels by cascading two identical building blocks. While this provides a useful proof of concept, the scheme could potentially be extended further for a more insightful discussion. In particular, cascading non-identical building blocks may enable a richer set of discrete levels and more versatile control.
Some small remarks for the authors’ consideration:
1. Some typos should be double-checked carefully, i.e. in the abstract the word "reconfiguable" should be “reconfigurable”.
2. In Fig. 1b, the annotation “Two degenerate subspace” is recommended to be corrected as “Two degenerate states” or “Two-dimensional degenerate subspace”. Similar descriptions, such as “Three degenerate subspace” in the annotation of Fig. 1b and “the number of degenerate spaces” in the caption of Fig. 1, are also recommended to be revised.
3. In the sentence “This creates slight color contrasts between the recrystallized region and the original crystalline substrate, as seen in Supplementary Fig. 2a,” it appears that the referenced image should be Fig. 2a in the main text rather than the supplementary material. Please verify and correct this reference for clarity and consistency.
4. The unit of the scale bar in Fig. 1d should be provided.
5. The symbol “μ” in Supplementary Eq. (S3) should be well defined.

### Reviewer 2

This work demonstrates in-memory multilevel control of generic SO(m) holonomy using a multilayer silicon photonic platform integrated with the phase-change material Sb₂Se₃. By optically switching the Sb₂Se₃ waveguides between amorphous and crystalline states, the authors dynamically modulate the number of degenerate modes in the system, enabling reconfigurable non-Abelian geometric phases without volatile external controls. They experimentally achieve high-fidelity, nonvolatile SO(2) and SO(3) transformations, along with tunable two- and three-mode braiding operations, and showcase multi-level programmability through cascaded SO(2) units and Givens rotations. This approach merges the inherent robustness of geometric phases with the nonvolatile tunability of PCMs, offering a promising pathway toward fault-tolerant photonic quantum processing, reconfigurable optical switching networks, and high-dimensional classical neuromorphic computing.
In my opinions, this work demonstrates the first experimental realization of reconfigurable control over non-Abelian holonomy, which exhibits notable innovation. However, several issues should be addressed prior to publication:
1. First and foremost, regarding novelty, this work combines the concepts of "reconfigurability" and "non-Abelian holonomy," which brings to mind two related works also published in Nature Communications: Nat. Commun. 16, 7089 (2025) and Nat. Commun. 16, 3650 (2025). Compared to the former, this study extends braiding operations to more general holonomic scenarios and introduces a new refractive index tuning method; compared to the latter, it achieves dynamic control over the SO(m) group. The authors should provide more detailed and specific comparisons with these relevant works, and include necessary discussions in the manuscript to better highlight the originality and significance of their contribution.
2. As a follow-up to the point above, different to Nat. Commun. 16, 7089 (2025), which employs the thermo-optic effect for active tuning, this work utilizes the phase-change material, claiming advantages in lower energy consumption and improved stability. The authors are encouraged to provide a detailed comparison of the advantages and disadvantages of different active tuning methods to underscore the technical and systemic innovation of their approach.
3. While the active tuning strategy presented is appealing, it remains limited to switching between SO(2) and SO(3) based on the presence or absence of onsite index mismatch. It would be valuable if the authors could discuss whether their method can be extended to design more complex or interesting functionalities.
4. The caption of Figure 2e is overly brief. A more detailed explanation of how the SO(2) transformation is realized in parameter space should be provided to assist readers unfamiliar with the process of non-Abelian holonomy.
5. The multilayer quasi-3D waveguide platform constructed using deposited SiO₂ is a promising architecture. However, a valid concern is whether next-nearest-neighbor coupling coefficients (such as κCD) can be neglected in such multilayer waveguides, and whether they might disrupt the holonomy process. Supplementary data on coupling coefficients should be provided in the Supplementary Information of this work to facilitate reader understanding.
6. Several minor issues require attention: the parameter space vectors on lines 91 and 136 contain a square symbol on the left-hand side of the equation, which may be a display error. The matrix alignment in Eq. (1) is also irregular. The authors should correct these and carefully check for other similar issues throughout the text.

with different volume fractions. As the material transitions toward either a fully
amorphous or fully crystalline state, the refractive index variation significantly
diminishes, in accordance with the Arrhenius law. Since our 100 nm-thick PCM is
very close to complete phase-transition, it can be considered free of notable
nonuniformity or resulting gradient, and this does not impede its reversible switching.

intermediate states with a mixed state of amorphous and crystalline phases. However,
the performance of the photonic devices primarily depends on the effective refractive
index of the entire waveguide. Even with minor variations in the refractive index
configuration due to random crystallization, the non-Abelian geometric phase remains
inherently unaffected due to its intrinsic tolerance to parameter fluctuations and
robustness against perturbations. This ensures stable and reliable performance despite
minor variations, making such devices highly practical for advanced applications in
photonics and quantum technology.

Response:
We are very thankful for the reviewer’s instructive comments. Indeed, both
thermal turning and non-volatile tuning are important active tuning approaches.
However, we believe that phase-change materials (PCMs) offer some advantages over
conventional thermo-optic (TO) modulation in integrated photonic devices,
particularly in terms of refractive index contrast, non-volatility, and no thermal
crosstalk, as will be discussed in detail below.
(i) Large refractive index contrast. PCMs exhibit drastic changes in optical
properties between amorphous and crystalline phases, with refractive index
differences (Δn) exceeding 0.7 in the near-infrared regime. In contrast, TO effects
induce only small index changes (typically ~10-2). The large refractive index contrast
facilitates significant onsite index matching or mismatching, enabling the complete
and stable switching from a three-fold degeneracy to a two-fold degeneracy, and
thereby supporting reconfigurable holonomic evolution paths.
(ii) Ultra-low power consumption and non-volatility. A key advantage of
PCMs is their non-volatile nature: once switched, the state is retained without power.
Energy is consumed only during the transient switching event (fJ to pJ per bit). In
contrast, TO devices require continuous power to maintain a state, resulting in high
static power consumption and thermal crosstalk.
(iii) Absence of thermal crosstalk. Thermal crosstalk is a notable problem of
thermo-optic modulation in high-density programmable integrated photonics. The
persistent heat diffuses laterally through the substrate and dielectric layers, altering
the refractive index of neighboring waveguides. Especially for the non-Abelian
holonomy with densely packed waveguides, thermal crosstalk makes independent
control of nearest-neighboring waveguides challenging. Evident thermal crosstalk
may influence the degeneracy of tunable SO(2) holonomy. As Fig. R14a shows, [Nat.
Commun. 16, 7089 (2025)] also simulates the influence of thermal crosstalk in
reconfigurable braiding, and the propagation constant of neighboring waveguide X
slightly varies as the distance to the electrode. Fig. R14b shows the temperature
distribution observed in an integrated thermo-optic modulation device, captured using
a thermal imaging camera (FOTRIC 280+). Evident thermal crosstalk can be
observed in the spot point (Sp1). In contrast, PCM is non-volatile with no static heat,
and its switching heat is transient and highly localized, enabling crosstalk-free,
independent tuning of individual waveguides within the holonomy, and preventing
degradation of the degeneracy caused by thermal crosstalk.
